sections.h2: Which offices run property tax inside Morris County?
sections.html:
Morris County splits the job between a county board and 39 town offices. The Morris County Board of Taxation holds the county's records of taxable real estate, sets tax rates and equalization ratios, supervises the municipal assessors, reviews assessments and rules on appeals. Its mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900.

New Jersey leaves budgets to local government, and the state receives none of the property tax money. A town divides the dollars it must raise by the assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders, and that quotient is the general rate. Your bill equals the rate times your own assessment (NJ Division of Taxation).

  • Your town's assessor sets the number printed on your notice.
  • The county board hears disputes about that number and publishes each town's rate.
  • The county clerk records the deed after a sale.

sections.h2: How pricey and how owner heavy are Morris County homes?
sections.html:
Morris County is wealthy and mostly owner occupied. Census QuickFacts puts the 2025 population estimate at 524,251, up from 509,285 in the 2020 count, with 193,245 households averaging 2.62 people. Few households move in a given year, since 91.1 percent of residents stayed at their address over the prior twelve months.

Owners without a mortgage still carry $1,385 a month, and a large share of that is the tax bill and insurance. Nearly 58 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and the average commute is 29.8 minutes, which tells you most buyers are professionals who work elsewhere in the New York area.

sections.h2: What should a home seller know about the Morris County landscape?
sections.html:
Morris County sits about 30 miles west of New York City. Morristown is the seat, and the county has many commuter towns and no big city. Parsippany-Troy Hills is the most populous municipality at 56,162 people in 2020, and Rockaway Township covers the most ground at 45.55 square miles. Roughly 4.3 percent of the county's 481.52 square miles is water.

The land climbs from the flatter Passaic River valley suburbs in the east to hills in the west. The highest point, 1,395 feet, is in western Jefferson Township. The Rockaway River drains 125 square miles of the north, the Whippany River drains 69 square miles through the middle, and the South Branch of the Raritan and the Black River drain the west. A house on a valley floor and a house on a ridge face different drainage questions, so ask your town about flood mapping before you set an asking price.

The housing stock carries history. The Continental Army wintered at Jockey Hollow in 1779 and 1780, and Dover was an iron mining center in the 1880s. Older houses in those towns often need more work than a newer subdivision, and that gap shapes what a buyer will pay for a home sold as it stands. The county's per capita income was the highest in New Jersey in 2021, which keeps renovation expectations high.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Morris County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the Morris County Board of Taxation, and have the petition in its hands by April 1, or May 1 in a town that just revalued. The Division of Taxation's form A-1 and the comparable sales sheet go in together (NJ Division of Taxation).

The county board holds that your value counts as excessive only when it misses a yardstick. After a revaluation, the yardstick is 100 percent of market value on the previous October 1. In other years, the town's common level range is the yardstick, set at plus or minus 15 percent around its average ratio.

  • Use arm's length sales dated before October 1.
  • Plan to appear in person, because the board runs no virtual hearings.
  • A losing owner can go next to the Tax Court of New Jersey within 45 days of the judgment.
  • Assessments above $1,000,000 can skip the county board and go straight to the Tax Court.
  • Added or omitted assessments use form AA-1, with direct Tax Court access above $750,000.

sections.h2: Which relief programs end when a Morris County owner sells?
sections.html:
Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ cover only a principal residence, so a sale generally closes them out for that address. A homeowner aged 65 or older can hold all three, while renters can use ANCHOR alone. The state's posted application deadline was November 2, 2026, and it has passed (Division of Taxation FAQ).

The Division's home sale guide adds two cautions for movers. Say on the application that you moved after October 1, or the benefit can be lost. Anyone in Senior Freeze who buys another New Jersey home waits two years, instead of three, for a new base year.

Separate local deductions exist for seniors and disabled persons and for veterans, along with an exemption for disabled veterans. Your town's tax office administers those, so ask whether the break on your Morris County house stops at closing.

sections.h2: What happens at the table when a Morris County house sells?
sections.html:
The seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee at recording and files a GIT/REP form with the deed. A resident seller signs GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated income tax payment, and gain is reported on the NJ-1040 later. Rates are on the Division's Realty Transfer Fee page.

Deeds are recorded by the Registry Department of the Morris County Clerk. Every land document needs a cover sheet and a cover letter with the submitter's name and address, plus a "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return" note on the document. The Registry takes recordings between 8:00 AM and 4:00 PM and can be reached at 973-285-6130.

Ask your town's tax office for a payoff on any unpaid quarter. Ask the closing attorney for the proration of the current year's bill. Those two numbers decide your net from a Morris County sale.

sections.h2: What does the Morris County job base mean for buyers?
sections.html:
Morris County has 16,518 employer establishments and about 301,249 jobs, with a 2023 payroll near $29.8 billion. Health care and social assistance brought in $6.83 billion in 2022 receipts, and retail sales reached $12.3 billion, or $24,110 per resident. Employment grew 1.9 percent from 2022 to 2023.

A deep local job market means a house that is priced to the county's $582,500 typical value usually draws interest from buyers who already work nearby. Houses that need a new roof or an estate cleanout draw a narrower pool, so those sellers often weigh a sale as is against months of repair work.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Morris County property tax appeal?
faqs.a: File with the Morris County Board of Taxation, using Form A-1 and the comparable sales form. The board's mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900, and hearings take place in person.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Morris County tax appeal?
faqs.a: The petition must be received by April 1, or by May 1 where the municipality completed a revaluation or reassessment. The Division of Taxation treats the date as a receipt deadline, so mail early.

faqs.q: Does Morris County bill my property tax?
faqs.a: No, your municipality bills and collects it. The county board sets rates and equalization ratios and hears appeals, while your town's tax office issues the bill and supplies payoff figures at a sale.

faqs.q: Can I skip the county board if my house is assessed above $1,000,000?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner whose assessment is above $1,000,000 may file directly with the Tax Court of New Jersey, and the filing must still be received by April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer fee on a Morris County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it, and it is collected at recording. A separate graduated percent fee also lands on the seller when the price tops $1,000,000.
